record.original_question: What are the best possible lower and upper bounds for the i-th adjacency eigenvalue of an n-vertex graph?

evidence.quote: Problem 11 (Hong [84]). Find the best possible lower and upper bounds for the i-th eigenvalue of graphs with n vertices.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on $n$ vertices with adjacency matrix $A(G)$, and let its eigenvalues be ordered as
$$\lambda_1(G) \ge \lambda_2(G) \ge \cdots \ge \lambda_n(G).$$
For each fixed integer $i$ with $1 \le i \le n$, determine the best possible (i.e., sharp) lower and upper bounds
$$L(n,i) \le \lambda_i(G) \le U(n,i)$$
that hold for every simple graph $G$ on $n$ vertices, where
$$U(n,i) = \max_{|V(G)|=n} \lambda_i(G), \qquad L(n,i) = \min_{|V(G)|=n} \lambda_i(G),$$
and characterize the extremal graphs that attain these bounds.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is classical (Hong, 1993). For $i=1$ and $i=2$ the sharp bounds are known, and for the smallest eigenvalues there are well-known results, but for general intermediate $i$ with $2 < i < n$ the exact best-possible bounds remain unresolved. Nikiforov and others have obtained partial results and constructions (e.g., based on Taylor's strongly regular graphs and Hadamard-matrix constructions), showing in particular that natural asymptotic bounds of order $\sim n/i$ are exceeded for $i \ge 5$. The general problem is still considered open.

status_evidence.title: Extrema of graph eigenvalues
status_evidence.snippet: In 1993 Hong asked what are the best bounds on the k'th largest eigenvalue of a graph of order n. This challenging question has never been tackled for any 2 < k < n.
status_evidence.claim: Hong's problem on the k-th largest eigenvalue of an n-vertex graph remains untackled for 2<k<n.

status_evidence.title: Graph Eigenvalues and Projection Constants
status_evidence.snippet: This problem of finding the exact values of c_k goes back at least to Powers and Hong, and was placed in a systematic framework by Nikiforov. Tight bounds are obtained for all k > 2.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work provides tight (but not always exact) bounds toward Hong's problem, indicating only partial progress.
